newsitem.title: UK: Julie Christie joins UK union in Disney protest.
newsitem.headline: Julie Christie joins UK union in Disney protest.

text.p: British actress Julie Christie joined British union workers on Wednesday to protest against business practises at Walt Disney Co which they allege lead to the exploitation of workers and children in Haiti.

The star of blockbuster movie Doctor Zhivago visited Disney's Regent Street store to hand over a letter calling on Disney chief executive Michael Eisner to end what the GMB union claimed were "abusive" conditions faced by workers.

"These clothes and products are the result of exploitation of people in countries such as Haiti who are very vulnerable. We are talking about starvation wages," Christie, a member of the Haiti Support Group, told Reuters. In a written statement, Disney said it was extremely careful about the conditions under which its products were made. It said it required that no child labour be used.

"In Haiti, an inspection and review has demonstrated that we are adhering to all applicable laws and policies. Workers who make Disney licensed goods do so in decent conditions and are being paid above the local minimum wage," Disney said.
The Haiti Support Group alleged workers employed by Disney sub-contractors found their wages covered less than a quarter of their basic needs and workers needed to go into debt to survive.

In the letter to Eisner, the GMB General Union claimed Haitian workers who produced Disney products earned as little as four pence (six cents) an hour to produce items retailing at 12 pounds (twenty dollars) and were denied the opportunity to discuss wages.

Christie, whose latest movie role is in Kenneth Branagh's Hamlet, said she hoped the protest would highlight the plight of Odette Denier, a worker sacked after organising a union at BVF Apparel, a Haitian company producing goods for Disney.

"I don't think great multinationals, especially those as powerful as Disney should think they can get away with exploiting people in far-flung areas of the world in order that we are able to receive cheap luxury goods," Christie said.
The GMB union called on Disney, known for its wholesome image and family-oriented theme parks, to become a world leader in protecting human rights and wiping out worker abuse.

"The last thing we want is Disney to stop business in Haiti but we expect them to set a standard. They could double wages without any impact on profit and immeasurably improve the lives of Haiti's people," GMB national secretary Des Farrell said.
"We are not saying boycott Disney but we are saying people should think carefully about making purchases and should be able to ask where products are made," Farrell said.

Disney Store spokesman Marco Ferrari declined to comment on the protest and referred all questions to the written statement. The British protest follows a campaign in the U.S. by the National Labor Committee to highlight Disney business in countries with questionable human rights records.
